summary.text: Writing the rank in terms of \(F_n=\lfloor e^{H_n}\rfloor\), the proof shows \(1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\) (using direct exponential estimates for the first few indices and \(H_n<\log n+2/3\) thereafter), so \(F_{n+1}-F_n\in\{1,2\}\) and hence each rank difference is 2 or 3. Telescoping gives the respective densities as \(e^\gamma-1\) and \(2-e^\gamma\), so the ratio tends to \((e^\gamma-1)/(2-e^\gamma)\); bounds \(16/9<e^\gamma<41/23\), obtained from harmonic/Euler–Mascheroni approximants at 1024 and explicit exponential-series estimates, place this limit strictly between 3.5 and 3.6.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j
\]
be the \(n\)-th harmonic number, and put
\[
F_n=\left\lfloor e^{H_n}\right\rfloor.
\]
We first express the rank in terms of \(F_n\).

For fixed \(n\), exactly \(n\) harmonic sums \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\) are at most \(H_n\), since the harmonic sums are strictly increasing. Moreover,
\[
\log(k+1)<H_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k+1<e^{H_n}.
\]
There are therefore \(F_n-1\) logarithmic terms preceding \(H_n\). There is no equality between a harmonic number and one of these logarithms: \(H_n\) is a nonzero rational number, and the Hermite–Lindemann theorem implies that \(e^{H_n}\) is transcendental, hence cannot equal the integer \(k+1\). Consequently the rank of \(H_n\) in the jointly ordered list is
\[
a(n)=n+F_n-1. \tag{1}
\]
This also agrees with the equivalent expression
\(n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\), because \(e^{H_n}\) is not an integer.

We next prove the key estimate
\[
1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\qquad(n\ge 1). \tag{2}
\]
Since \(H_{n+1}=H_n+1/(n+1)\),
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
=e^{H_n}\left(e^{1/(n+1)}-1\right). \tag{3}
\]

For the lower bound, the standard integral comparison for the harmonic sum gives
\[
\log(n+1)\le H_n.
\]
Thus \(e^{H_n}\ge n+1\). Also \(e^x>1+x\) for every nonzero real \(x\), so
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}-1>\frac1{n+1}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities in (3) yields
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}> (n+1)\frac1{n+1}=1.
\]

We now prove the upper bound in (2). First suppose \(n\ge6\). The sequence
\[
U_n=H_n-\log n\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
is strictly decreasing. Indeed,
\[
U_{n+1}-U_n
=\frac1{n+1}-\log\left(1+\frac1n\right)<0,
\]
because \(\log(1+t)>t/(1+t)\) for \(t>0\). At \(n=6\),
\[
H_6=\frac{49}{20},
\qquad
H_6-\log6<\frac23.
\]
The last inequality is equivalent to \(e^{107/60}<6\), and follows directly by bounding the exponential series; all terms are positive and the remaining tail is bounded by a geometric majorant. Hence, for \(n\ge6\),
\[
H_n<\log n+\frac23,
\qquad
e^{H_n}<n e^{2/3}. \tag{4}
\]
A direct exponential-series estimate gives
\[
e^{2/3}<2. \tag{5}
\]

For \(0<x<1\), another elementary exponential estimate is
\[
e^x<\frac1{1-x}. \tag{6}
\]
For example, this follows by comparing
\(e^x=\sum_{j\ge0}x^j/j!\) with the geometric series
\(\sum_{j\ge0}x^j=1/(1-x)\), with strictness because \(1/j!<1\) for \(j\ge2\). Taking \(x=1/(n+1)\) gives
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}-1
<\frac{1}{1-1/(n+1)}-1
=\frac1n. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (3), (4), and (7), we obtain
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
<n e^{2/3}\cdot\frac1n
=e^{2/3}<2.
\]
Thus the upper bound is proved for \(n\ge6\).

It remains only to check \(1\le n<6\). We record the elementary exponential estimates used in this finite check:
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{1/2}&<\frac53,&
 e^{1/3}&<\frac75,&
 e^{1/4}&<\frac97,\\
e^{1/5}&<\frac{11}{9},&
 e^{1/6}&<\frac65,&
 e^{17/60}&<\frac43,\\
e^{1/12}&<\frac{11}{10},&
 e^{5/6}&<\frac73,&
 e&<\frac{68}{25}<3.
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
Each inequality in (8) is an elementary rational check from the exponential series. One convenient uniform certificate is the following: for \(0\le x\le1\) and an integer \(m>0\),
\[
e^x\le \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{x^j}{j!}
 +\frac{x^m(m+1)}{m!m}.
\]
Substitution gives the displayed inequalities; one may use respectively \(m=5,8,8,8,8,10,8,30\), while the familiar series estimate for \(e\) gives \(e<68/25\).

Now use (3) and the exact values
\[
H_1=1,\quad H_2=\frac32,\quad H_3=\frac{11}{6},
\quad H_4=\frac{25}{12},\quad H_5=\frac{137}{60}.
\]
For \(n=1\), (8) gives
\[
e^{H_1}<3,
\qquad e^{1/2}-1<\frac23,
\]
so the product in (3) is less than \(3(2/3)=2\).

For \(n=2\),
\[
e^{H_2}=e\,e^{1/2}<3\cdot\frac53=5,
\qquad e^{1/3}-1<\frac25,
\]
so the product is less than \(5(2/5)=2\).

For \(n=3\),
\[
e^{H_3}=e\,e^{5/6}<3\cdot\frac73=7,
\qquad e^{1/4}-1<\frac27,
\]
so the product is less than \(7(2/7)=2\).

For \(n=4\), write \(25/12=1+1+1/12\). Then
\[
e^{H_4}<\left(\frac{68}{25}\right)^2\frac{11}{10}<9,
\qquad e^{1/5}-1<\frac29,
\]
and hence the product is less than \(9(2/9)=2\).

Finally, for \(n=5\), write \(137/60=1+1+17/60\). Then
\[
e^{H_5}<\left(\frac{68}{25}\right)^2\frac43<10,
\qquad e^{1/6}-1<\frac15,
\]
so the product is less than \(10(1/5)=2\). This completes the proof of (2).

We now pass from (2) to the floor increments. We use the elementary fact that if \(x\ge0\) and
\[
1<y-x<2,
\]
then
\[
\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\{1,2\}. \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, from \(x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\) and \(y>x+1\) we get
\(y>\lfloor x\rfloor+1\), and therefore
\(\lfloor y\rfloor\ge\lfloor x\rfloor+1\). On the other hand,
\(x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\) and \(y<x+2\) imply
\(y<\lfloor x\rfloor+3\), so
\(\lfloor y\rfloor\le\lfloor x\rfloor+2\). This proves (9).

Apply (9) with \(x=e^{H_n}\) and \(y=e^{H_{n+1}}\). By (2),
\[
F_{n+1}-F_n\in\{1,2\}\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{10}
\]
Using (1),
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)=1+F_{n+1}-F_n. \tag{11}
\]
It follows immediately from (10) that every successive difference is either \(2\) or \(3\).

We next determine the asymptotic ratio of these two kinds of differences. Let \(C_3(N)\) and \(C_2(N)\) denote respectively the number of \(3\)'s and \(2\)'s among
\[
a(2)-a(1),\ldots,a(N+1)-a(N).
\]
By (10)–(11), a difference of \(a\) is \(2\) precisely when the corresponding increment of \(F\) is \(1\), and it is \(3\) precisely when that increment is \(2\). Therefore
\[
C_2(N)+C_3(N)=N, \tag{12}
\]
and, by telescoping,
\[
C_2(N)+2C_3(N)
=\sum_{n=1}^N(F_{n+1}-F_n)
=F_{N+1}-F_1. \tag{13}
\]
Solving (12) and (13) gives the exact formulas
\[
C_3(N)=F_{N+1}-F_1-N, \tag{14}
\]
\[
C_2(N)=2N-(F_{N+1}-F_1). \tag{15}
\]
The nonnegativity of the right sides also follows directly by summing the lower and upper bounds \(1\le F_{n+1}-F_n\le2\).

Let \(\gamma\) denote the Euler–Mascheroni constant. The classical harmonic-number limit is
\[
H_n-\log n\longrightarrow\gamma. \tag{16}
\]
Exponentiating (16), and using \(e^{H_n}/n=e^{H_n-\log n}\), gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_n}}n\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{17}
\]
Because
\[
e^{H_n}-1<F_n\le e^{H_n},
\]
division by \(n\) and squeezing show that
\[
\frac{F_n}{n}\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{18}
\]
Since \((N+1)/N\to1\), (18) also yields
\[
\frac{F_{N+1}}N\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{19}
\]
Dividing (14) and (15) by \(N\), noting that the fixed quantity \(F_1/N\) tends to zero, we obtain
\[
\frac{C_3(N)}N\longrightarrow e^\gamma-1, \tag{20}
\]
\[
\frac{C_2(N)}N\longrightarrow 2-e^\gamma. \tag{21}
\]

It remains to show both that the limit in (21) is positive and that the quotient of (20) and (21) lies between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\). For this we establish the rational bounds
\[
\frac{16}{9}<e^\gamma<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{22}
\]

We give the finite estimates underlying (22). The two standard Euler–Mascheroni approximants are
\[
L_n=H_n-\log(n+1),\qquad U_n=H_n-\log n.
\]
The first is strictly increasing and the second strictly decreasing. Their difference is
\(\log(n+1)-\log n\to0\), so they have the common limit \(\gamma\), and for every positive \(n\),
\[
H_n-\log(n+1)<\gamma<H_n-\log n. \tag{23}
\]
The monotonicity follows from the elementary logarithmic inequalities
\[
\frac{t}{1+t}<\log(1+t)<t\qquad(t>0).
\]

At \(n=1024\), exact summation of the rational number
\(H_{1024}=\sum_{j=1}^{1024}1/j\) gives
\[
\frac{75091}{10000}<H_{1024}<\frac{75092}{10000}. \tag{24}
\]
This is simply a finite rational comparison after bringing the sum to a common denominator.

The exponential-series estimate stated above, together with positivity of its terms, gives
\[
2.7182818283<e<2.7182818286, \tag{25}
\]
\[
e^{5091/10000}>\frac{1663}{1000}, \tag{26}
\]
and
\[
e^{5092/10000}<\frac{3329}{2000}. \tag{27}
\]
For (26), summing through degree \(19\) and bounding the error through degree \(20\) suffices; for (27), the corresponding upper estimate through degree \(29\), with the degree-\(30\) remainder bound, suffices. All comparisons are between explicit rational numbers.

Since \(75091/10000=7+5091/10000\), (24)–(26) imply
\[
e^{H_{1024}}
> (2.7182818283)^7\frac{1663}{1000}
>\frac{16}{9}\,1025. \tag{28}
\]
Likewise, since \(75092/10000=7+5092/10000\), (24), (25), and (27) imply
\[
e^{H_{1024}}
<(2.7182818286)^7\frac{3329}{2000}
<\frac{41}{23}\,1024. \tag{29}
\]
The last inequalities in (28) and (29) are direct integer arithmetic after replacing each terminating decimal by its defining rational number. Numerically, the intermediate left side in (28) exceeds \(1823.70\), whereas \((16/9)1025=1822.22\ldots\); the intermediate upper bound in (29) is less than \(1825.346\), whereas \((41/23)1024=1825.391\ldots\).

Exponentiating (23) at \(n=1024\) gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_{1024}}}{1025}<e^\gamma<
\frac{e^{H_{1024}}}{1024}.
\]
Combining this with (28) and (29) proves (22).

In particular, \(e^\gamma<41/23<2\), so \(2-e^\gamma>0\). We may therefore divide the limits (20) and (21), obtaining
\[
\frac{C_3(N)}{C_2(N)}
=\frac{C_3(N)/N}{C_2(N)/N}
\longrightarrow
L:=\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}. \tag{30}
\]
(The denominator is nonzero for all sufficiently large \(N\), since its normalized value tends to the positive number \(2-e^\gamma\).)

Finally, for any \(x<2\), elementary rearrangement with the positive denominator \(2-x\) gives
\[
\frac{x-1}{2-x}>\frac72
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x>\frac{16}{9},
\]
and
\[
\frac{x-1}{2-x}<\frac{18}{5}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x<\frac{41}{23}.
\]
Taking \(x=e^\gamma\) and using (22), we conclude that
\[
3.5=\frac72<L<\frac{18}{5}=3.6.
\]
Together with (11), this proves both assertions: every successive difference is \(2\) or \(3\), and the ratio of the number of \(3\)'s to the number of \(2\)'s among the first \(N\) differences tends to a limit strictly between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\).
